This tutorial covers the process of detecting and mapping trees, as well as classifying their live/dead status and genus/species, from processed drone data.

{{ pagetree(siblings) }}

docs.title: Task 1: Detection & mapping
docs.text: We will use the OFO's Tree Detection Framework to detect and delineate tree crowns from drone-derived data products using a variety of approaches, including a geometric algorithm applied to a canopy height model (CHM) and several different computer vision algorithms applied an orthomosaic.

docs.title: Required input data
docs.text: Name Source Example file Canopy height model Photogrammetry post-processing composite1_chm-mesh.tif Orthomosaic Photogrammetry post-processing composite1_ortho-dsm-ptcloud.tif

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Before you begin, make sure you have gone through the OFO tutorial preparation guidance. We recommend running OFO tools via their Docker images. Follow our Docker guide to understand what Docker is and ensure your system is set up to run Docker containers. If instead you plan to run the tools in a local Python environment, follow the local installation instructions to set up a Conda environment for the following tools:

  • Tree Detection Framework

docs.title: Geometric tree detection from a canopy height model
docs.text:
First, we will use a geometric algorithm implemented in the Tree Detection Framework to detect treetops as local maxima in the canopy height model (CHM). This approach uses a variable-radius local maximum filter. We will demonstrate with the CHM linked above:

DockerJupyterPython command-line entrypointPython script

Linux/Mac:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
    -v "${DATA_DIR}:/data" \
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-detection-framework:latest \
    python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.detect_geometric_two_stage \
        /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif \
        /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg \
        --tree-crowns-save-path /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_geometric_v01.gpkg \
        --raster-blur-sigma 0.5 \
        --tree-top-detector-kwargs '{"a": 0, "b": 0.0325, "c": 0.25, "min_ht": 5}'

Windows:

docker run --rm `
    -v "${env:DATA_DIR}:/data" `
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-detection-framework:latest `
    python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.detect_geometric_two_stage `
        /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif `
        /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg `
        --tree-crowns-save-path /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_geometric_v01.gpkg `
        --raster-blur-sigma 0.5 `
        --tree-top-detector-kwargs '{\"a\": 0, \"b\": 0.0325, \"c\": 0.25, \"min_ht\": 5}'

This step is performed by the TDF Geometric Detector example notebook. You can change the constants in the second cell. Ensure Jupyter is using the the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

In your terminal, activate the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

conda activate tree-detection-framework

Then run the geometric detection entrypoint script.

python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.detect_geometric_two_stage \
    ${DATA_DIR}/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif \
    ${DATA_DIR}/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg \
    --tree-crowns-save-path ${DATA_DIR}/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_geometric_v01.gpkg \
    --raster-blur-sigma 0.5 \
    --tree-top-detector-kwargs '{"a": 0, "b": 0.0325, "c": 0.25, "min_ht": 5}'

Run the following code from within the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

from pathlib import Path

from tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.detect_geometric_two_stage import detect_trees_two_stage

# Change this line
DATA_DIR = Path("path/to/data")

# Define the inputs
CHM_PATH = Path(DATA_DIR, "photogrammetry-postprocessed", "full", "composite1_chm-mesh.tif")
TREE_TOPS_SAVE_PATH = Path(DATA_DIR, "output", "detected-trees", "composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg")
TREE_CROWNS_SAVE_PATH = Path(DATA_DIR, "output", "detected-trees", "composite1_tree-crowns_geometric_v01.gpkg")
RASTER_BLUR_SIGMA = 0.5
TREE_TOP_DETECTOR_KWARGS = {"a": 0, "b": 0.0325, "c": 0.25, "min_ht": 5}

# Run detection
detect_trees_two_stage(
    CHM_file=CHM_PATH,
    tree_tops_save_path=TREE_TOPS_SAVE_PATH,
    tree_crowns_save_path=TREE_CROWNS_SAVE_PATH,
    raster_blur_sigma=RASTER_BLUR_SIGMA,
    tree_top_detector_kwargs=TREE_TOP_DETECTOR_KWARGS,
)

This command saves two geospatial output files: points representing detected tree tops and polygons representing detected tree crowns. You can visualize these outputs in GIS software like QGIS:

The detected trees all have a height attribute extracted from the CHM by Tree Detection Framework. The heights were used to size the tree points in the visualization above.

The geometric tree detection algorithm can be parameterized in many different ways. For example, the value passed to raster-blur-sigma controls the amount of smoothing applied to the CHM before detecting local maxima. The values given for a, b, and c in the tree-top-detector-kwargs affects the local maximum search radius relative to the height of the tree. Other parameters not supplied here (and thus using their defaults) include chip_size and chip_stride, which control how large CHMs are split up into manageable chunks prior to processing, and resolution, which controls the resolution the CHM is resampled to prior to running the algorithm. See the Tree Detection Framework documentation for a detailed description of all parameters. Here is an example of the effect of setting the treetop detector parameter c to 5.

The Open Forest Observatory has done extensive testing of the geometric tree detection algorithm and has found that the default parameters used here work well in many California conifer forests. Some of our parameter tuning work is published in Methods in Ecology and Evolution , and other work is in progress.

docs.title: Computer vision tree detection from an orthomosaic
docs.text:
The Tree Detection Framework also provides an interface to several existing computer vision models for detecting trees from an orthomosaic. These models run fastest when a GPU is available, but some can also run on a CPU in a reasonable amount of time, particularly for small orthomoaics.

We will first demonstrate using it to run DeepForest on the orthomosaic linked above:

DockerJupyterPython command-line entrypointPython script

Running without a GPU

If you are running this on a machine without a GPU, remove --gpus all from the docker run command below.

Linux/Mac:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
    --gpus all  --group-add "$(stat -c %g /dev/nvidia0)" \
    -v "$DATA_DIR:/data" \
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-detection-framework:latest \
    python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.generate_predictions \
        --raster-folder-path /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_ortho-dsm-ptcloud.tif \
        --tree-detection-model deepforest \
        --chip-size 1024 \
        --chip-stride 768 \
        --resolution 0.05 \
        --run-nms \
        --predictions-save-path /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg

Windows:

docker run --rm `
    -v "${env:DATA_DIR}:/data" `
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-detection-framework:latest `
    python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.generate_predictions `
        --raster-folder-path /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_ortho-dsm-ptcloud.tif `
        --tree-detection-model deepforest `
        --chip-size 1024 `
        --chip-stride 768 `
        --resolution 0.05 `
        --run-nms `
        --predictions-save-path /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg

This step is performed by the TDF tree detection example notebook. Note that the constants in cell 2 will need to be changed to reflect the data used in this documentation. Ensure Jupyter is using the the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

In your terminal, activate the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

conda activate tree-detection-framework

Then run the prediction generation entrypoint script.

python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.generate_predictions \
    --raster-folder-path ${DATA_DIR}/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_ortho-dsm-ptcloud.tif \
    --tree-detection-model deepforest \
    --chip-size 1024 \
    --chip-stride 768 \
    --resolution 0.05 \
    --run-nms \
    --predictions-save-path ${DATA_DIR}/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg

Note that you can replace deepforest with detectree2 to run that model.

Run the following code from within the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

from pathlib import Path

from tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.generate_predictions import (
    generate_predictions,
)

# Change this line
DATA_DIR = Path("path/to/data")

# Define the inputs
RASTER_FOLDER_PATH = Path(DATA_DIR, "photogrammetry-postprocessed", "full", "composite1_ortho-dsm-ptcloud.tif")
TREE_DETECTION_MODEL = "deepforest"
CHIP_SIZE = 1024
CHIP_STRIDE = 768
RESOLUTION = 0.05
RUN_NMS = True

# Define the outputs
PREDICTIONS_SAVE_PATH = Path(DATA_DIR, "output", "detected-trees", "composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg")

# Run detection
generate_predictions(
    raster_folder_path=RASTER_FOLDER_PATH,
    predictions_save_path=PREDICTIONS_SAVE_PATH,
    tree_detection_model=TREE_DETECTION_MODEL,
    chip_size=CHIP_SIZE,
    chip_stride=CHIP_STRIDE,
    resolution=RESOLUTION,
    run_nms=RUN_NMS,
)

This step saves a geospatial file of polygons (rectangles) representing the bounding boxes of detected tree crowns. You can visualize these outputs in GIS software like QGIS:

The rectangle bounding box output format is specific to the DeepForest model.

Since geospatial rasters are often large, we cannot assume that a computer vision model can generate predictions for the whole raster at once. Instead, the raster is broken up into smaller chips, and an independent prediction is generated on each one. These predictions are subsequently merged back together. The chip_size and chip_stride parameters, both in pixels, represent the chip dimensions and how much the sliding window moves between each chip. The computer vision models may produce overlapping detections, and the run_nms argument controls whether the non-max suppression algorithm should be run to only retain the highest-confidence detection if multiple overlap. Finally, the resolution parameter controls the size in meters of a single pixel in the chip, and the original data is resampled on the fly to achieve this. In practice, this parameter has a large impact on the performance of models and specifically what size of tree is detected well. By coarsening the resolution to 0.2m, only the largest trees are detected, as visualized below.

The Tree Detection Framework provides a standardized interface to several different methods of performing tree detection, taken from the literature. TDF handles the process of chipping a raster into smaller chips, generating predictions on each chip, and merging these predictions back together in one command, so this complexity is abstracted from the user, and end-to-end workflows are easy to run. A key benefit of TDF is the ability to quickly compare multiple models, while holding key pre- and post-processing parameters consistent. TDF is also optimized for realistic-scale raster data, meaning that it can be directly applied to even the largest drone flights. A table of the supported approaches is below.

Method Learning Strategy Input Data Output Format DeepForest Task-specific training Orthomosaic Bounding box Detectree2 Task-specific training Orthomosaic Crown polygon Restor TCD Task-specific training Orthomosaic Crown polygon Segment Anything Model v2 (SAM2) Generic pretraining (foundational model) Orthomosaic Crown polygon Segment Anything Model v3 (SAM3) Generic pretraining, with class information (foundational model) Orthomosaic Crown polygon Local maximum filter + Watershed segmentation Learning-free algorithm Canopy height model (CHM) Tree-top point and crown polygon

To run detections using an alternative model, simply change deepforest in the command above to the name of the model you want to use.

To enable support for SAM3, you must follow the prompts here. This will require you to create a HuggingFace account if you do not have one already. After creating an account, you must wait for your request to be manually reviewed. Then go here, select Create new token, and select Token type Read. Enter an arbitrary name and create the token. Copy the token and store it somewhere, since you won't be able to see its value after creating it. Finally, add it to the list of arguments when running the SAM3 model:

--sam3-huggingface-token SAM3_HUGGINGFACE_TOKEN

docs.title: Generating tree top points from computer vision detections
docs.text:
The computer vision tree detection approaches do not product a point representation of trees by default. However, tree top points are required for matching detected trees to ground reference trees, as demonstrated in the Evaluation tutorial. TDF provides a tool to generate tree top points from computer vision crown polygons.

DockerPython command-line entrypointPython script

Linux/Mac:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
    -v "$DATA_DIR:/data" \
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-detection-framework:latest \
    python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.polygons_to_points \
        --detections-path /data/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg \
        --chm-path /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif \
        --output-path /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01-tree_points_chm-max.gpkg \
        --method chm_max

Windows:

docker run --rm `
    -v "${env:DATA_DIR}:/data" `
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-detection-framework:latest `
    python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.polygons_to_points `
        --detections-path /data/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg `
        --chm-path /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif `
        --output-path /data/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01-tree_points_chm-max.gpkg `
        --method chm_max

In your terminal, activate the tree-detection-framework Conda environment.

conda activate tree-detection-framework

Then run the polygons to points script script.

python -m tree_detection_framework.entrypoints.polygons_to_points \
    --detections-path ${DATA_DIR}/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01.gpkg \
    --chm-path ${DATA_DIR}/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif \
    --output-path ${DATA_DIR}/output/detected-trees/composite1_tree-crowns_deepforest-bbox_v01-tree_points_chm-max.gpkg \
    --method chm_max

docs.title: Task 2: Classification
docs.text:
Our goal here is to predict the species and live/dead status of every detected tree using computer vision applied to the raw drone photos. To do this, we will use the OFO tools Geograypher and Tree Classification Framework and an OFO fork (modification) of MMPretrain, an external tool that simplifies running computer vision models.

We will use all of the views of each detected tree from each drone photo it appears in. Because the raw drone photos are not geospatial data products, some intermediate processing using OFO tools is required. The process follows this workflow:

  • Use Geograypher to render the unique ID of each detected tree to the perspective of each image it appears in
  • Use the Tree Classification Framework to crop out each view of each tree from each drone photo it appears in, while preserving the unique ID of the tree
  • Use the OFO fork of MMPretrain to generate a prediction of species and live/dead status for each individual tree crop
  • Use the Tree Classification Framework to aggregate the predictions for each individual tree crop into a single geospatial prediction for each detected tree.

To translate between geospatial coordinates (detected trees) and raw drone photos, we will need 3D models of the site derived from processing the raw photos using photogrammetry.

The detected tree crowns may be ones you produced in the Detection task, or you can use the pre-generated detections in the tutorial data folder (linked above). It is important that the detections and photogrammetry camera locations be derived from the same photogrammetry run, using the same raw drone photos that you will use for this task.

docs.title: Rendering tree locations to images
docs.text:
The first step in classifying trees is use Geograypher to understand what region of each image observes each tree--or at a lower level, where in 3D geographic space is a given pixel from a raw drone image. The first two inputs are from photogrammetry: (a) the 3D structure of the scene represented as a mesh model, and (b) the location and orientation from which each image was captured, produced by photogrammetry as an XML file. Additionally, the digital terrain model (DTM) (derived from post-processing photogrammetry products) is used in this particular application for determining which part of the mesh represent the ground. Finally, we require the 2D geospatial locations of the detected tree crowns, obtained using a detection algorithm such as those demonstrated in Task 1.

Fortunately, if we know the precise location of the camera sensor at at the time each image is captured (which we obtain from photogrammetry), along with the parameters of the camera's lens (also from photogrammetry), then we can use geometry to translate each pixel in a raw drone image into a ray in 3D space. The place where this ray intersects the 3D mesh model is the location in 3D space that is represented by that pixel. Geograypher uses techniques from computer graphics to perform these calculations efficiently. Notably, this rendering process is occlusion-aware, so if one tree is in front of another from the camera's perspective, the pixel will be assigned to the tree in front.

Each tree is assigned a unique numeric ID when it is detected. Since the mesh model has geospatial reference information, these IDs can be transferred from the 2D geospatial representation of the crowns to the corresponding 3D mesh faces. Then, we use Geograypher to assign those IDs to the corresponding pixels in each raw drone image. This produces a single-channel image encoding the ID of the observed tree (or a special background ID) at each pixel, for each image in the original set of drone images.

The original drone images are not required at this stage except for visualization.

docs.title: Crop the view of each tree from each drone photo
docs.text:
The previous step identified the location of each tree in each image, but additional processing is required to prepare this data for a computer vision prediction model. Specifically, we use a classification model, which takes an image and produces a single label. To accommodate this format, we must create one image per view of each tree. Using the rendered mask from Geograypher, a rectangular region surrounding each observed tree is cropped from the original image. Then, any content within the crop but outside the bounds of the tree is set to a background color. Finally, each chip is written out, while preserving both the structure of the image it was derived from and the ID of the tree it was generated from.

docs.title: Assign predictions to individual trees
docs.text:
The end goal of this process is to obtain a tree-level class prediction for each tree. Each tree is likely to have been observed many times, from different viewpoints, and will therefore have multiple classification results. We maintain the tree's unique ID through all steps in the process, so the view-level predictions still tie back to a specific tree. Since predictions may differ across views, we take the modal (most common) prediction across all views, and assign this as the predicted tree label. This information is then joined with the geospatial crown information that was originally used to generate the chips, then saved out (as a new geospatial file). In addition to the predicted class, we also include the number of views which contributed to the prediction and the fraction of views that agreed with the modal prediction. These attributes are suffixed with _n_preds and _frac_matching_mode, respectively, and may be used in downstream tasks to filter out low-confidence predictions.

docs.title: Evaluating tree detection accuracy
docs.text:
This tutorial covers the process of evaluating the accuracy of automated geospatial tree detections by comparing the detections against ground-based plot data.

{{ pagetree(siblings) }}

docs.title: Task 1: Co-registration
docs.text: For many applications, we may wish to compare the results of drone-based tree detection and classification against ground reference data. However, before we can do any comparison, we need to make sure the two datasets are spatially co-registered (aligned).

docs.title: Required input data
docs.text: Name Source Example file Canopy height model Photogrammetry post-processing composite1_chm-mesh.tif Ground reference trees (geospatial points) Manual fieldwork ofo-ground-reference-trees_0030.gpkg

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Before you begin, make sure you have gone through the OFO tutorial preparation guidance. We recommend running OFO tools via their Docker images. Follow our Docker guide to understand what Docker is and ensure your system is set up to run Docker containers. If instead you plan to run the tools in a local Python environment, follow the local installation instructions to set up a Conda environment for the following tools:

  • Tree Registration and Matching Toolkit

docs.title: Dataset co-registration using height correlation
docs.text:
Although both the drone imagery and reference tree locations are usually georeferenced with GPS/GNSS, each set of measurements can have an independent bias due to GPS/GNSS error (e.g., atmospheric distortions, signal attenuation by the tree canopy) at the time of survey. This creates a spatial offset, commonly on the order of several meters, between the two sets of data. An example of this phenomenon can be seen below, where the field reference trees (blue points) are shifted upward and slightly left relative to the corresponding drone trees represented by the CHM. The white line represents the bounds of of the ground plot, showing the region within which trees were surveyed.

The OFO has developed the Tree Registration and Matching Toolkit (TRAM) to automatically identify the spatial registration between two datasets. The specific algorithm we will be using here registers a set of ground reference trees (geospatial points) to a drone-derived CHM (a geospatial raster). TRAM also contains algorithms to register two sets of geospatial points (e.g., ground reference trees and drone-detected trees).

The algorithm use will use to align the drone and reference data takes the CHM and ground reference tree locations (with a height attribute for each tree) as input. The algorithm extracts the height value from the CHM at each reference tree location, then computes the correlation between the reference tree heights and the CHM-derived heights. It then shifts the reference tree locations across a grid of offsets in both the x and y directions, and at each offset, re-computes the height correlation. The result is a grid of correlation values, where the maximum correlation indicates the optimal shift to align the two datasets.

The commands to run this algorithm are below.

        --CHM-file /data/photogrammetry-postprocessed/full/composite1_chm-mesh.tif \
        --tree-points-file /data/ground-reference/ofo-ground-reference-trees_0030.gpkg \

Now the surveyed tree tops match up much better with the drone CHM. While there are some errors, these errors are in different directions for every tree, so no single shift would improve all trees dramatically. Some small amount of tree-level error is always expected, due largely to human error during ground survey and the fact that ground surveyed tree locations (tree stems) are not always directly under the tree tops. In the next task, we will see that despite these errors, we can use a simple matching algorithm to identify the tree-to-tree correspondences between the two datasets.

docs.title: Task 2: Evaluation
docs.text: The final task is assessing the quality of the detected trees. This is done by comparing the locations of detected trees to those of field reference trees after co-registering the datasets (Registration task). This process produces metrics quantifying the fraction of real trees the detection algorithm found ("recall"), the fraction of detected trees that were real ("precision"), and a combined metric (F1) that balances the two. The evaluation process also produces a visualization of the matched trees, which can be used to identify patterns in the errors made by the detection algorithm.

You may similarly provide your own ground reference trees file, as long as it contains an attribute named height for each tree, or use the pre-prepared file in the tutorial data folder.

docs.title: Detection evaluation with spatial tolerance
docs.text:
The tree detection evaluation algorithm quantifies how well the detected trees correspond to the ground reference trees. Does every detected tree correspond to a real tree observed on the ground? Does every real tree have a corresponding detected tree? To answer these questions, we need to pair the detected trees with their corresponding ground reference trees. However, due to random spatial error in both the drone and ground reference datasets, corresponding trees are never exactly co-located. Therefore, we allow a spatial tolerance in determining whether a detected tree corresponds to a ground reference tree. The spatial tolerance is a function of the height of the ground reference tree, with taller trees having a larger tolerance. This approach, published in Methods in Ecology and Evolution , accounts for the fact that taller trees are morely likely to have a lean or complex crown morphology such that the tree top (the point detected by drone) is not directly above the stem (the point mapped in the ground survey).

The spatial tolerance could, in some cases, allow a given ground tree to match to more than one drone tree or vice-versa. To avoid this, the algorithm uses a greedy matching approach which identifies the best (spatially closest) match between the two datasets, then removes those trees from further matching, then computes the next best match, and so on until all trees have been matched or no more matches can be made.

Once all matchable trees are matched, it is then possible to compute the evaluation metrics based on the number of trees and the number that were matched, in both the drone and ground datasets. When scoring, it is necessary to exclude spatial edge effects (e.g. a drone tree just inside the plot bounds that corresponded to a real field tree that was just outside the plot bounds and was therefore not recorded). To account for this, the scoring process only asks about matches for trees that are inset at least 5 m from the plot bounds, and which are over 10 m in height.

The commands to run this algorithm are shown below.

DockerPython command-line entrypointPython script

Linux/Mac:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
    -v "${DATA_DIR}:/data" \
    ghcr.io/open-forest-observatory/tree-registration-and-matching:latest \
    python -m tree_registration_and_matching.entrypoints.score_detected_trees \
        /data/ground-reference/ofo-ground-reference-trees_0030.gpkg \
        /data/detected-trees/composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg \
        /data/ground-reference/ofo-ground-reference-plot_0030.gpkg \
        --shift-file /data/registration/reference-drone-registration.csv \
        --output-file /data/output/detection-evaluation/tree-scoring-metrics.json \
        --vis-file /data/output/detection-evaluation/tree-scoring-matches.png

    -v "${env:DATA_DIR}:/data" `

In your terminal, activate the tree-registration-and-matching Conda environment.

conda activate tree-registration-and-matching

Then run the tree detection scoring entrypoint script.

python -m tree_registration_and_matching.entrypoints.score_detected_trees \
    ${DATA_DIR}/ground-reference/ofo-ground-reference-trees_0030.gpkg \
    ${DATA_DIR}/detected-trees/composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg \

Run the following code from within the tree-registration-and-matching Conda environment.

from pathlib import Path

from tree_registration_and_matching.entrypoints.score_detected_trees import score_detected_trees

# Change this line
DATA_DIR = Path("path/to/data")

# Define the inputs
FIELD_TREES_FILE = Path(DATA_DIR, "ground-reference", "ofo-ground-reference-trees_0030.gpkg")
DRONE_TREES_FILE = Path(DATA_DIR, "detected-trees", "composite1_tree-tops_geometric_v01.gpkg")
FIELD_PLOT_BOUNDS_FILE = Path(DATA_DIR, "ground-reference", "ofo-ground-reference-plot_0030.gpkg")
SHIFT_FILE = Path(DATA_DIR, "registration", "reference-drone-registration.csv")

# Define the outputs
OUTPUT_FILE = Path(DATA_DIR, "output", "detection-evaluation", "tree-scoring-metrics.json")
VIS_FILE = Path(DATA_DIR, "output", "detection-evaluation", "tree-scoring-matches.png")

metrics = score_detected_trees(
    field_trees_file=FIELD_TREES_FILE,
    drone_trees_file=DRONE_TREES_FILE,
    field_plot_bounds_file=FIELD_PLOT_BOUNDS_FILE,
    shift_file=SHIFT_FILE,
    output_file=OUTPUT_FILE,
    vis_file=VIS_FILE,
)
print(metrics)

This saves out a map image depicting the detected and reference trees and the matches between them. Ground reference trees are indicated in light blue, drone-detected trees are in red, and the matches between them are in pink. The plot boundary is shown in white.
